title: Maternal smoking in pregnancy and birth defects: a systematic review based on 173 687 malformed cases and 11.7 million controls

subsections.subsection_title: Biological Rationale and Reproductive Toxicity Mechanisms
subsections.content:
The biological plausibility linking maternal smoking to congenital anomalies is strong because cigarette smoke delivers a complex mixture of nicotine, carbon monoxide, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, oxidants, metals, and other toxicants to the maternal-fetal unit ref [2]. These exposures can disrupt organogenesis through several overlapping pathways: fetal hypoxia from carbon monoxide and vasoconstriction, oxidative stress, DNA damage, apoptosis, altered cell signaling, and impaired placental development and transport ref [2], ref [3], ref [4]. Experimental work further indicates that tobacco toxicants can perturb proliferation, migration, and differentiation in embryonic and extraembryonic tissues, processes central to craniofacial, cardiac, and limb morphogenesis ref [2], ref [5], ref [6].

A vascular-placental mechanism is particularly relevant. In pregnant smokers, endothelial function is measurably impaired, with reduced flow-mediated dilatation and an association between maternal endothelial dysfunction and fetal growth restriction ref [1]. Histologic and in vitro studies also show smoking-related injury in placental villi and umbilical vessels, including altered cytotrophoblast differentiation, reduced invasion, endothelial degeneration, and disturbed angiogenic signaling ref [1], ref [7], ref [8], ref [9], ref [10]. Such changes support the concept that chronic uteroplacental underperfusion may accompany direct embryotoxicity, thereby amplifying susceptibility during critical windows of development.

Specific constituents offer additional mechanistic insight. Nicotine can alter uterine and uterine-artery contractility and impair placental trophoblast function, while carbon monoxide reduces oxygen delivery; together these may restrict nutrient and oxygen supply during early development ref [2], ref [11], ref [12]. Meanwhile, PAHs and related compounds activate aryl hydrocarbon receptor pathways, induce Bax-dependent apoptosis, and damage germ and embryonic cells in vitro, consistent with teratogenic and developmental toxicity ref [2], ref [5], ref [13]. These mechanisms do not establish defect specificity on their own, but they provide a coherent toxicologic framework for the epidemiologic associations reviewed in subsequent sections.

subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiologic Overview of Maternal Smoking and Congenital Anomalies
subsections.content:
Epidemiologic investigation of maternal smoking and congenital anomalies initially yielded inconsistent results, largely because early studies were small, retrospective, or analyzed heterogeneous malformation groups as a single outcome. A hospital-based case-control study reported a modest excess for all malformations combined that was concentrated among women smoking more than 20 cigarettes per day, with evidence of dose-response and higher risks across several defect categories rather than one isolated phenotype ref [5].

By contrast, large prospective cohorts generally found little or no increase in overall major malformations. In two prospective U.S. datasets comprising 86,946 live births, Shiono et al. concluded that smoking was unlikely to produce a large increase in malformations at birth; most initially significant subtype associations were not replicated across cohorts, although inguinal hernia appeared more consistent ref [4]. Population monitoring data from Mainz likewise emphasized the importance of registry-based ascertainment and regional surveillance, documenting substantial background frequencies of both major and minor anomalies while supporting multivariable assessment of prenatal risk factors ref [7].

More recent cohort evidence has reinforced the view that any teratogenic signal from maternal smoking is modest overall but may vary by defect class and study design. In the Danish National Birth Cohort, smoking during the first 12 weeks was not associated with an increase in total congenital malformations and showed no dose-response gradient, although elevations were noted for some specific categories such as cleft lip/palate and cardiovascular defects ref [6]. Interpretation of this literature depends heavily on exposure and outcome measurement: studies of birth-certificate smoking data show that misclassification can attenuate associations and distort effect estimation, underscoring the need for prospectively collected smoking histories and high-quality defect registries ref [6].

subsections.subsection_title: Defect-Specific Evidence: Craniofacial, Cardiac, Limb, and Musculoskeletal Outcomes
subsections.content:
Defect-specific evidence indicates that associations with maternal smoking are not uniform across congenital anomalies but are concentrated in several phenotypes. For craniofacial outcomes, the evidence is strongest for oral clefts: a meta-analysis reported modest but significant elevations for cleft lip with or without cleft palate and cleft palate alone, with evidence of a dose-response pattern in several contributing studies ref [8]. Large population-based analyses likewise found increased odds of cleft lip/palate among smokers, with risk rising across cigarette-consumption categories ref [10]. Maternal smoking has also been linked to craniosynostosis, where case-control data suggested an overall excess risk and particularly strong associations for heavier smoking and coronal synostosis ref [7].

For congenital heart defects, evidence is more subtype-specific than global. In the National Birth Defects Prevention Study, periconceptional smoking was associated most clearly with septal defects, especially atrial septal defects, and with right-sided obstructive lesions at heavier exposure levels, whereas environmental tobacco smoke showed little association ref [9]. This phenotype specificity is consistent with earlier reports suggesting elevated risks for selected cardiac subgroups rather than a uniform increase across all CHDs ref [9].

Limb and musculoskeletal findings show a similar pattern of selective vulnerability. Maternal smoking has been associated with congenital digital anomalies, with elevated odds for polydactyly, syndactyly, or adactyly and evidence of increasing risk with greater cigarette use ref [10]. Studies of limb deficiency also reported positive associations, particularly for reduction-type defects ref [8]. In musculoskeletal outcomes, idiopathic talipes equinovarus has shown one of the more reproducible smoking signals, including dose-related increases and stronger estimates in isolated cases ref [12]. Taken together, these data support the view that smoking-related teratogenicity is defect-specific, modest in magnitude, and potentially strongest for anomalies plausibly linked to vascular disruption, hypoxia, or impaired tissue fusion and patterning ref [8], ref [12], ref [7], ref [8].

subsections.subsection_title: Susceptibility, Gene-Environment Interaction, and Related Developmental Outcomes
subsections.content:
Susceptibility to smoking-related teratogenesis is unlikely to be uniform across pregnancies. A key line of evidence comes from gene-environment studies of detoxification pathways in orofacial clefting, where maternal smoking shows stronger effects in the presence of specific fetal or maternal variants in xenobiotic-metabolizing genes. In a large Danish-Iowa analysis, smoking displayed dose-related associations with clefting, while fetal GSTT1-null status significantly modified smoking-related risk and suggestive effects were also reported for NAT2 and CYP1A1; embryonic craniofacial expression data further supported biologic plausibility for GSTT1-mediated susceptibility ref [13]. Earlier studies likewise implicated GSTT1, GSTM1, EPHX1, NAT1/NAT2, and related biotransformation genes as modifiers of smoking-associated oral cleft risk, although replication has been uneven and some signals remain modest or population-specific.

These findings fit a broader framework in which inherited variation may influence activation, detoxification, placental transfer, oxidative stress handling, and fetal tissue response to tobacco constituents. The literature on clefts provides the clearest example, but the same conceptual model is relevant to other anomaly groups and may help explain heterogeneity across epidemiologic studies. At the same time, many candidate-gene reports were small, vulnerable to multiple-testing problems, and often lacked independent replication; thus, apparent interactions should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating unless supported across populations or by functional data ref [13].

Related developmental outcomes also inform susceptibility assessment. Maternal smoking does not appear to materially alter the birth prevalence of Down syndrome overall, based on meta-analytic evidence, with a pooled relative risk close to unity; however, smoking substantially shifts second-trimester screening analytes, lowering free beta-hCG and uE3 while increasing AFP and especially inhibin-A, thereby affecting risk estimation and screening comparability between smokers and non-smokers ref [4]. This distinction is important for review framework purposes: smoking may influence developmental biomarkers and ascertainment processes even when it is not a causal determinant of a given chromosomal condition ref [4].

subsections.subsection_title: Review Framework: Confounding, Data Quality, and Nutritional Modifiers
subsections.content:
Interpretation of associations between maternal smoking and congenital anomalies depends critically on how confounding is handled. Socioeconomic position, maternal age, parity, alcohol use, obesity, diabetes, family history of defects, and co-exposures such as medications can all distort smoking–defect estimates if incompletely measured. Nutritional behaviors are especially relevant because women who smoke differ systematically in supplement use and diet quality, and these differences may correlate with both case status and pregnancy loss. Studies of multiple congenital anomalies underscore that adjustment for education, gravidity, alcohol, smoking, body mass index, and family history can materially alter effect estimates, while also showing that residual confounding remains plausible when diet and other health behaviors are not fully captured [1], ref [16].

Data quality is an equally important review dimension. Smoking is often self-reported retrospectively and may be misclassified, particularly when ascertainment occurs months after delivery, or when case and control mothers differ in recall or social desirability bias. Outcome quality also varies with surveillance design, inclusion of stillbirths and terminations, diagnostic intensity, and the exclusion of recognized chromosomal or syndromic cases; these factors are especially consequential for heterogeneous multiple-anomaly phenotypes [1], ref [16]. More generally, validity studies have shown that routine vital-record smoking data can be inadequate for effect estimation, reinforcing the need to distinguish prospective exposure measurement, biomarker validation, and active defect ascertainment in evidence synthesis.

Nutritional modifiers should therefore be treated not only as confounders but also as potential effect modifiers. Periconceptional vitamins containing folic acid have established protective effects for neural tube defects and possible benefits for selected cleft, cardiac, urinary, and limb outcomes, yet studies of multiple anomalies have produced inconsistent findings, ranging from null results to positive associations [1], ref [16]. For smoking-focused reviews, this literature is useful because smoking lowers folate status and may interact with supplement use, background diet, or broader multivitamin-associated behaviors. A rigorous framework should thus evaluate adjustment for folic acid or multivitamin use, consider dietary folate misclassification, and remain alert to selection mechanisms related to fetal survival, which could influence the observed birth prevalence of malformations among smokers and non-smokers alike [1], ref [16].

Assessment of evidence robustness in this literature begins with exposure ascertainment, because most studies of maternal smoking and congenital anomalies rely on maternal self-report recorded at prenatal booking, delivery, or postpartum interview. The central concern is nondifferential and, in some settings, socially patterned underreporting of smoking, which can attenuate risk estimates and distort dose-response analyses. Direct validation work shows that self-report during pregnancy underestimates true smoking prevalence when compared with biochemical markers: in a Scottish population, cotinine validation indicated a 17% excess of smokers beyond self-report, with greater misclassification in more deprived groups, highlighting both measurement error and its unequal distribution across populations [2].

This problem is particularly salient for birth-defects epidemiology because exposure windows of etiologic interest are often periconceptional or limited to the first trimester, whereas smoking status is frequently captured later in gestation or abstracted from birth records. Studies comparing data sources have shown that birth certificate smoking variables have imperfect sensitivity for effect estimation, especially for lighter smokers and subgroup analyses, and that agreement between interview, medical record, and administrative data is incomplete [8]. Broader perinatal epidemiology likewise reports only moderate concordance between self-reported smoking and biomarkers such as serum, urine, or salivary cotinine, with under-ascertainment influenced by stigma, timing of assessment, and cessation or reduction after recognition of pregnancy [2].

Accordingly, the most credible associations are those reproduced across designs with different exposure ascertainment strategies or those robust to likely exposure misclassification. Because underreporting of active smoking during pregnancy is generally expected to bias results toward the null rather than create spurious positive associations, persistent excess risks observed across registry-based, interview-based, and case-control studies remain informative even when absolute exposure prevalence is underestimated [8]. Nevertheless, future studies would be strengthened by repeated measurement across early gestation, finer characterization of intensity and quitting trajectories, and routine biochemical validation in at least a subsample to permit quantitative bias analysis and improve comparability across populations [2].

Biological plausibility for a teratogenic contribution of maternal smoking is supported by convergent vascular, cellular, and developmental evidence. In pregnant smokers, markedly reduced flow-mediated dilatation indicates persistent endothelial dysfunction, and lower maternal endothelial function has been linked with fetal growth restriction, consistent with impaired uteroplacental perfusion and oxidative vascular injury as core pathways of fetal harm ref [1]. Reviews of placental pathology similarly describe smoking-related vascular lesions, abnormal villous morphology, and altered placental development, reinforcing a mechanism in which chronic hypoxia, vasoconstriction, and endothelial injury disturb embryofetal oxygen and nutrient delivery.

Mechanistic support is strengthened by experimental studies showing that tobacco smoke is not a single-agent exposure but a complex mixture that can disrupt multiple reproductive targets. In vitro systems demonstrate adverse effects on ovarian follicles, oocyte maturation, fallopian tube function, uterine contractility, placental trophoblast proliferation and invasion, umbilical endothelial cells, and embryo development ref [2]. Specific constituents—including nicotine, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, cadmium, formaldehyde, acrolein, and pyridine/pyrazine derivatives—have been shown to impair ciliary activity, alter cell migration, induce apoptosis, suppress steroidogenesis, and inhibit trophoblast differentiation ref [2]. Experimental evidence that PAHs activate aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling and Bax-dependent germ-cell apoptosis, and that nicotine can retard postimplantation embryonic growth and induce oxidative-stress-mediated apoptosis, provides a mechanistic bridge from maternal exposure to abnormal morphogenesis ref [2].

These mechanisms are especially relevant to structural malformations because organogenesis depends on tightly regulated cell proliferation, migration, fusion, and vascular remodeling. Smoking-related perturbation of neural crest cell behavior, extracellular matrix interactions, and tissue oxygenation offers biologically credible explanations for associations reported for orofacial clefts, some cardiac defects, and limb reduction patterns. Although direct defect-specific experimental models remain incomplete, the overall mechanistic record strongly supports causality as biologically plausible rather than merely statistical.

Across defect categories, the epidemiologic literature is more notable for recurring signal patterns than for universal uniformity. Associations are strongest and most reproducible for selected phenotypes rather than for birth defects as a single aggregate outcome. For congenital heart defects, population-based analyses have linked periconceptional smoking to septal defects and some right-sided obstructive lesions, with evidence of higher risks at heavier smoking levels ref [8]. This aligns with earlier registry-based findings for atrial septal defects and selected outflow tract phenotypes, although effect sizes vary across studies and not all cardiac subgroups are consistently implicated.

A similarly patterned consistency is seen for craniofacial outcomes. Maternal smoking has repeatedly been associated with orofacial clefts, and the association is strengthened in studies showing dose-response gradients ref [13]. The persistence of this finding across Danish and U.S. populations, together with prior meta-analytic synthesis of case-control and cohort studies, supports the view that the cleft association is not a single-study artifact. Importantly, heterogeneity by cleft subtype remains expected, with cleft lip with or without cleft palate generally showing more stable associations than cleft palate only ref [13].

Overall, the epidemiologic record supports a moderate but credible teratogenic signal for maternal smoking, characterized by phenotype specificity, modest effect sizes, and occasional dose-response relations rather than broad uniform elevation across all malformations ref [8], ref [13]. Inconsistencies across studies are plausibly explained by differences in case classification, exposure timing, smoking intensity, covariate control, and susceptibility-genotype distributions; thus, partial heterogeneity should be interpreted as refinement of the association rather than evidence against it.

Comparative evidence is useful for judging whether the smoking–birth defect associations are specific, biologically coherent, and of plausible public-health importance rather than isolated statistical findings. One relevant contrast comes from periconceptional folate research: unlike the strong preventive effect of folate on neural tube defects, evidence for non-neural defects such as orofacial clefts, heart defects, urinary tract defects, and limb reduction defects has been mixed or null in some population studies, underscoring that congenital anomaly risks are exposure-specific and mechanistically heterogeneous rather than uniformly responsive to maternal nutritional or toxic exposures ref [18]. This contextualizes smoking findings by showing that different teratogens and preventive factors map onto different defect spectra.

A second contextual layer is disease burden. Defects repeatedly linked with maternal smoking in epidemiologic studies—especially orofacial clefts and some cardiac or limb anomalies—are not trivial endpoints. In US hospital data, selected birth defects are associated with substantial neonatal hospital stays, charges, and in-hospital mortality, highlighting that even modest relative risk elevations may translate into meaningful healthcare burden at the population level ref [19]. For orofacial clefts specifically, downstream consequences extend beyond infancy to quality of life, psychosocial functioning, long-term morbidity, and sustained healthcare utilization and costs ref [20]. Thus, comparative burden data strengthen the significance of smoking-related associations even when effect sizes are moderate.

Broader contextual evidence also argues against interpreting the smoking literature in isolation. Orofacial clefts show socioeconomic patterning and are influenced by multiple prenatal factors, including folate-related pathways and other maternal behaviors, which emphasizes the need to assess smoking within a wider causal network rather than as a sole determinant ref [18], ref [20]. At the same time, the large clinical and economic burden attached to these outcomes means that residual confounding cannot simply dismiss observed associations; instead, it elevates the importance of triangulating evidence across etiologic, preventive, and health-services literatures. Overall, comparative and contextual findings support the view that maternal smoking is one modifiable contributor within a multifactorial framework, with potentially important implications for prevention and resource allocation ref [19], ref [20].

Supplementary materials in this literature are especially important because pooled estimates depend heavily on transparent reporting of study selection, defect classification, exposure ascertainment, and sensitivity analyses. Across the smoking–birth-defect literature, authors frequently differ in whether they report isolated versus multiple anomalies, live births only versus pregnancy losses, and crude versus adjusted estimates, all of which can materially affect synthesis and interpretation ref [3], ref [8], ref [4], ref [6], ref [7], ref [14], ref [15]. Detailed appendices are therefore essential for documenting search strategies, coding rules, and harmonization decisions.

Authorship information also bears directly on interpretability. Large population-based surveillance studies, registry linkages, and multicenter case-control investigations often involve epidemiologists, teratologists, statisticians, pediatric specialists, and birth-defect surveillance teams, reflecting the interdisciplinary nature of causal assessment in this field ref [12], ref [13], ref [11], ref [9], ref [10], ref [16], ref [1]. Clear attribution of roles in data curation, exposure validation, outcome adjudication, and meta-analytic methods improves reproducibility and helps readers assess potential sources of bias, particularly where self-reported smoking, birth certificate data, or biomarker validation are used ref [5], ref [17], ref [2].

For a systematic review of maternal smoking and congenital anomalies, the most valuable supplementary files typically include the full extraction table, defect-specific forest plots, quality or risk-of-bias assessments, subgroup definitions, and influence analyses excluding studies with weaker exposure measurement or atypical ascertainment windows ref [21], ref [22], ref [23]. Disclosure statements, funding information, and author-contribution notes are likewise nontrivial, because they contextualize methodological choices and support appraisal of whether conclusions about specific anomalies—such as heart defects, oral clefts, limb defects, and craniosynostosis—are robust across designs and investigative groups ref [8], ref [9], ref [10], ref [1], ref [24].
